spreads.scene: TWO PEOPLE MEETING is the subject, and there is NO handshake. DAVID KOBROSKY has just arrived in front of a young woman with box-braids and a mustard cardigan beside the snack table at frame LEFT, and he is welcoming her: his signature gesture, one open palm turned warmly UPWARD at waist height and the other arm sweeping gently toward the room behind him, as if to say the whole party was waiting for her. Her hands stay on her own paper cup, held close, her shoulders just unknotting. They stand FACING EACH OTHER, close, each in warm three-quarter view, HIS EYES LOCKED ON HER EYES AND HERS ON HIS, both mid-smile, hers just breaking into relief. His feet, hips, shoulders and gaze all point AT HER; nobody walks anywhere and nobody reaches for anybody. Behind them at frame RIGHT three other guests chat in a loose knot, faces angled away. The room is a warm rented hall dressed like a friend's dinner: string lights sagging overhead, a snack table with pretzel bowls and a lemonade jug, folding chairs, name tags, golden lamp light. The lower-right quarter of the frame stays calm: empty wooden floor with soft light. If the two of them do not read as meeting each other's eyes, the image is wrong.
spreads._caption: Every room has someone standing near the snack table who knows nobody. David finds them first. He crosses the room with his hand already out and says the four words he was born to say. Let me introduce you.
spreads.anonymous: Four party guests: the braided woman in the mustard cardigan, a heavyset South Asian man in a green polo, an older white woman with silver hair, a slim Black man in a denim shirt. All visibly distinct from David; none wears a sky-blue button-down; none shares his face, hair, or beard.
negatives: either of them reaching for the other's hand
David walking, striding, or moving past her
David's gaze aimed anywhere but her eyes

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY chest-up, large in the frame at the viewer's RIGHT third, standing a clear step INSIDE the room, fully separate from every wall and doorway: warm wall and lamplight are visible AROUND his whole silhouette, and no part of his body touches, overlaps, or blends into the doorframe. He holds a coffee mug in both hands at chest height, head turned to scan the room beyond, expression warm and attentive rather than amused: the look of a host counting who has been left out. Past him, softly out of focus at frame LEFT, a small gathering: two people deep in conversation with each other, and further back, half in lamplight near the window, one man standing alone looking at his phone. The sharp subject is David's watching face. Bottom-right of frame is calm warm wall, uncluttered.
spreads._caption: Running communities taught David what most builders never learn. Nothing is obvious to a newcomer, and if you make people feel stupid you lose them. So he watches the edges of every room and asks one question. Who is falling through the cracks?
spreads.anonymous: Background guests, all soft-focus and visibly distinct from David: no sky-blue shirt on any of them. The man alone by the window is slight, red-haired, in a gray hoodie.

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY climbs the steps of a Brooklyn brownstone stoop in early golden morning, two paper grocery bags in his arms with a baguette and a bunch of bananas poking out, his face turned back over the street with his warm grin. Around him New York wakes: water towers on rooflines, fire escapes, steam from a corner cart, and on the sidewalk FIVE ANONYMOUS PASSERSBY walk in different directions, each looking at their own feet or phone, NONE of them looking at each other. The picture's quiet argument is that David is the only person in frame paying attention to people. Warm brick and cream sky, no neon, no skyline glamour shot. Lower-right: empty sidewalk, calm.
spreads._caption: David came up in New York City, where eight million people live close enough to touch and a young person can still go a whole year without being known. Striving strangers arrive every day with big plans and nobody to tell them to. David looked at that and set the table.
spreads.anonymous: Five commuters, visibly distinct from each other and from David: different builds, skin tones, ages, coats. None wears a sky-blue button-down; none looks at anyone.
negatives: passersby making eye contact with anyone

spreads.scene: A SMALL NEW YORK APARTMENT PACKED WITH SUNDAY-MORNING PEOPLE, and DAVID KOBROSKY at the tiny stove mid-flip, a pancake in the air above his pan, laughing toward the crowded table, HIS EYES ON HIS GUESTS. Around a table that is clearly too small: SIX young professionals and founders wedged onto folding chairs and a sagging couch, mismatched mugs, a syrup bottle, somebody's laptop shut under a plate. Two guests lean into conversation with each other, eyes meeting; another pair laugh over a shared phone photo; one newcomer at the edge is being waved in by a guest sliding over to make room. Morning light through one big window, radiator under it, a hand-lettered paper banner on the wall reading exactly BRUNCH CLUB in friendly marker capitals. Warm, crowded, joyful. Lower-right: worn wooden floor with a stray tote bag, calm.
spreads._caption: It started in his own apartment. Folding chairs, borrowed mugs, pancakes for whoever rang the bell. He called it Brunch Club, and on Sunday mornings his place filled with young professionals and founders who had been strangers on Saturday night.
spreads.anonymous: Six brunch guests, all in their twenties and thirties, visibly distinct: a South Asian woman in a denim jacket, a heavyset white man in a hoodie, a Black woman with short locs, an East Asian man in a flannel, a redheaded woman, a Latino man in a tee. None resembles David; none wears sky-blue.
negatives: any text besides the exact BRUNCH CLUB banner

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY, chest-up at his crowded kitchen counter, hands a tall fruit smoothie across to a guest whose hands are just receiving it, HIS EYES LOCKED ON THE GUEST'S EYES, both mid-laugh. The blender jug sits beside him with three more filled glasses lined up, each a different sunrise color. Behind him, slightly soft, a wall crowded with dozens of small pinned photographs of past brunches, years of them, and a small glass jar of wooden tokens on the shelf. The guest is seen from behind over their shoulder, softly out of focus. Warm morning light. Lower-right: countertop with a folded dish towel, calm.
spreads._caption: He ran Brunch Club for years, more than a hundred brunches in all, and he made the smoothies himself. Ask anyone who came. The room stayed small on purpose, the door stayed open anyway, and table by table he became the center of a certain kind of gravity in New York.
spreads.anonymous: One guest receiving the smoothie, seen mostly from behind: a young woman with a dark ponytail in a green cardigan, visibly distinct from David.

Desk-lamp warmth. The faces in the photographs are tiny and soft, no larger than a thumbnail, none of them a recognizable canon character. Lower-right: bare shelf wood, calm.

spreads.scene: A BUSTLING MID-2010s MEDIA OFFICE IN FULL SWING, and TWO MEN cross it together: DAVID KOBROSKY, college-young in his navy polo, carries a cardboard box stacked with a laptop and rolled posters, and beside him strides GARY VEE, his boss, stocky and electric in a dark crew-neck tee, mid-sentence, one arm flung toward the doorway he is steering David through. spreads._caption: Before building his own thing he was Gary Vee's first crypto hire, sent to explore the strangest new corner of the internet. The job taught him how crowds gather online, and how they scatter. He kept the lesson.
spreads.anonymous: Two background staffers in motion, visibly distinct from both named men: a woman with a red ponytail in a dark green tee, and a tall thin man with blond curls in a mustard sweater. Nobody else has short dark hair or a stubble beard; nobody wears navy or any blue shirt.

spreads.scene: NIGHT AFTER A BRUNCH, and TWO MEN sit on the SAME side of a small kitchen table, shoulder to shoulder, both leaning toward ONE OPEN LAPTOP squarely in front of them, ITS SCREEN FACING THE TWO OF THEM, their eyes on the screen together. DAVID KOBROSKY is on the left, mid-idea, one hand gesturing at the screen; his FRIEND, a young man with wavy chestnut hair, round glasses and a maroon crewneck, types as he grins. Around the laptop: index cards with red yarn between them, a cold cup of coffee, and this morning's clean stacked plates drying by the sink behind them. On one index card, in plain marker capitals, exactly the word MEETSUNDAY. Lamplight, warm and late. Lower-right: table wood and one pencil, calm.
spreads._caption: Then he tried to bottle it. With a friend he built software that did what he did at brunch, notice which two strangers ought to meet, and they named the first version MeetSunday, after the morning the magic kept happening on.
spreads.anonymous: The friend and cofounder figure: wavy chestnut hair, round glasses, maroon crewneck, clean-shaven, visibly distinct from David; he is an anonymous companion, no real likeness.
negatives: the laptop screen facing the camera

spreads.scene: A close overhead INSERT: two strong forearms with rolled sky-blue sleeves, DAVID's hands, pinning a length of red yarn between two index cards on a big cork board that fills the frame. The board carries a couple dozen index cards, each with a hand-drawn stick-figure face and a first name in plain handwriting, many already joined by yarn lines, a warm constellation of people. One card at the edge, not yet connected, sits slightly apart. Desk lamp light rakes across the cork. No screens, no computers: the software idea rendered as the corkboard it was born from. The card names are short common first names (AVA, SAM, LEO, NOOR, JUNE) in casual handwriting.
spreads._caption: The software worked the way his table worked. It learned which two strangers ought to meet, then made the introduction for him, a thousand times a night. When it grew up they gave it the only name that fit. It was called Intros. Of course it was.

spreads.scene: A VAST EMPTY EVENT HALL in pale early light, rows of empty folding chairs stretching away, and DAVID KOBROSKY small near the center aisle, sleeves rolled, setting a small box of blank name tags onto the first chair, his face calm and certain, EYES ON THE ROOM he is about to warm. A rolling cart beside him holds stacked mugs and a coffee urn. The hall reads cold in its emptiness, all pale wall and long shadow, while David and his little cart are the one pool of warm color. The picture's argument is a cold room meeting the person who knows how to warm one. Lower-right: bare floorboards and chair legs in soft shadow, calm.
spreads._caption: Investors wired real money so that more strangers could meet. The pitch was simple. Every new community starts cold, a room where nobody knows anybody yet, and David had spent years learning exactly how to warm one up.

spreads.scene: AN INFUSION SUITE MADE HUMAN. DAVID KOBROSKY sits in a recliner chair by a big window, chest-up and large in frame, a soft KNIT BEANIE where his curls would be, an IV line taped to his forearm and a slim laptop open ON HIS LAP with ITS SCREEN FACING HIM, his hands on the keys. He is thinner in the face and unmistakably HIMSELF: the grin is intact, aimed down at the work, undefeated. A warm blanket, a smoothie cup on the side table, afternoon light across the floor. The picture's argument is a spirit that did not take the season off. Lower-right: sunlit linoleum, calm.
spreads._caption: In the middle of the building years, his own body picked a fight. Stage four blood cancer, the kind that comes with twelve rounds of chemo. David did the rounds, kept a full head of plans if not of hair, and kept building all the way through.
negatives: gaunt hopelessness: the mood is quiet defiance

spreads.scene: THE BELL. DAVID KOBROSKY stands at the end-of-treatment bell mounted on the clinic wall, one hand on the pull cord mid-RING, his other fist raised, face thrown back in a huge open laugh. His hair is back as a SHORT dark regrowth of curls under no hat. Around him, THREE nurses in scrubs and TWO friends applaud and cheer, all eyes on HIM, one friend holding up a phone to film, another holding a small handmade sign that reads exactly CANCER FREE in marker capitals. Streamers, a balloon, afternoon light. Pure triumph, zero solemnity. Lower-right: clinic floor with a fallen streamer, calm.
spreads._caption: And here is the most David thing that has ever happened. Mid-chemo, he rallied hundreds of friends to help cover someone else's cancer treatment, and let the internet vote on his hairstyle before the razor took it. By November the scans came back clean. Cancer, meet David. Let me introduce you.

negatives: any legible text besides the exact sign CANCER FREE

spreads.scene: THREE PEOPLE CELEBRATING fill this small startup office, and the champagne pop is the moment. DAVID KOBROSKY stands at the center behind a cluttered desk, POPPING A CHAMPAGNE BOTTLE: the cork is mid-flight near the top of the frame, foam just cresting from the neck, his grin huge, one fist raised. His TWO teammates flank him, both turned toward him and the bottle, celebrating with him: on the LEFT a nerdy, brilliant-looking young East Asian man programmer with thick round glasses, a rumpled graphic tee and a laptop-stickered water bottle, laughing with both arms up; on the RIGHT a Latina woman programmer with curly dark hair tied back, a flannel over a tee, holding out two paper cups to catch the pour, mid-cheer. Exactly three people in the room, all eyes on the bottle and each other, nobody looking at the camera. The office is small and scrappy: whiteboard of diagrams behind them, sticky notes, a pizza box, desk plants, late-afternoon sun through the window. It reads as a tiny team that just got the phone call. Lower-right: the warm blur of a chair back, calm.
spreads._caption: The company worked, and a bigger one bought it. The sale proved a thing David had known for years. Bringing people together is real work, as real as steel or code, and it is worth real money.
spreads.anonymous: Two Intros teammates, visibly distinct from David: a nerdy young East Asian man programmer with thick round glasses and a graphic tee, and a Latina woman programmer in a flannel with curly hair tied back. Neither wears a sky-blue button-down; neither shares David's face or beard.
negatives: black-tie gala or ballroom: this is a scrappy startup office

spreads.scene: OVER-THE-SHOULDER SHOT: the camera looks over DAVID KOBROSKY's right shoulder from behind. The keyboard sits under David's hands. From the laptop's edges, SIX SMALL CORAL HOLOGRAPHIC SUB-AGENTS in glowing white sailor caps stream outward into the warm study beyond, each carrying something away: a wrapped parcel, a paper airplane of pages, a rolled blueprint, a ledger, a letter, a lantern. They cast light, not shadow. The dim cozy study glows around them: bookshelves, a desk lamp, framed prints. One calm person at the center of many small helpers carrying the hours outward. Keep the far lower-right corner in soft shadow, calm.

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY, full of purpose, walks toward a plain warm terracotta door set in a cream wall, seen in three-quarter view from his front-left so his face and grin stay visible. THE DOOR IS A STANDARD AMERICAN DOOR, drawn correctly: a full-size leaf about three feet wide and eighty inches tall, taller than David, sitting inside a visible painted frame. Its round brass knob is at WAIST HEIGHT, thirty-six to forty inches off the ground, inset a hand's width from the leaf's right edge, with the hinges on the left edge at the jamb. David's hand reaches for the knob AT HIS OWN WAIST, elbow bent, back straight. Beside the door, a small plain nameplate carries the single word ANTHROPIC in simple capital letters, spelled exactly A-N-T-H-R-O-P-I-C, mounted at eye level. Morning light falls across the wall. The street behind him is soft and ordinary: a bike rack, a planter of rosemary. No campus, no glass tower, no logo anywhere else. The door is humble and the man is glad. Lower-right: warm pavement, calm.
spreads._caption: So when an AI lab came calling, David did the math out loud. Of the companies that could do something about the risks of AI, Anthropic sits front and center. He chose the place where his effort would count the most, and he got to work.
negatives: any logo or text besides the single ANTHROPIC nameplate
a knob mounted on or against the door frame

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY stands at a long worktable in the center-left of a bright loft, and behind and above him a whole wall rises covered in SEVERAL DOZEN small warm pennants and index cards, each a different color, each carrying a tiny meaningless doodle-mark (never legible text): the ninety startups in his care. FIVE CORAL HOLOGRAPHIC SUB-AGENTS, each WEARING ITS GLOWING WHITE SAILOR CAP, ferry between the wall and his table: one climbing a ladder to pin a card, one carrying a rolled chart, two conferring over a clipboard, one saluting David for a new instruction. spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY kneels mid-span on a small handmade wooden footbridge over a creek at golden hour, fitting the NEXT PLANK into place with both hands: the bridge is complete behind him from the near bank, and ahead of him the remaining gap is spanned only by the beam he is building along, leading toward a far bank that is brighter, greener, morning-lit. A canvas tool bag and a few waiting planks rest behind him. He looks toward the far bank as he works, grinning like a man who can already see the other side. Rolling meadow, long light, swallows. The image argues one thing: the crossing is being CHOSEN and BUILT, plank by plank, on purpose. Keep the water at lower-right smooth and calm.
spreads._caption: Underneath the career sits the thing David actually believes. One of the finest human qualities is that we do not have to wait for our evolution. We can look at what we are, decide what we would rather become, and build the bridge on purpose. Intention, meet evolution. Let me introduce you.

spreads.scene: TWO PEOPLE fill this frame with one laugh: DAVID KOBROSKY and MIKAELA side by side on a wooden porch swing in late golden light, turned half toward each other. Mikaela is mid-laugh, curls loose, leaning into David's shoulder; David grins down at her, one arm along the swing's back behind her, his other hand holding hers. String lights just coming on above, jasmine on the porch rail, two lemonade glasses on the rail. Both faces fully legible and joyful. Nothing else asks for attention. Lower-right: the porch floorboards in warm shadow, calm.
spreads._caption: For the record, the introducer's own best chapter began the ordinary way, with two people meeting. David married Mikaela, and anyone who has watched them laugh together knows the theory holds. Good rooms, good companies, good lives. Each one starts with the right introduction.

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY stands at a rooftop garden rail at dusk, back three-quarter to the viewer's LEFT edge with his face in warm profile-adjacent three-quarter view looking out, one hand open toward the view as if introducing it. Below and beyond spreads a warm neighborhood: a dozen pools of gathering light: a backyard dinner, a lit church hall, a rooftop movie, a garage workshop, porches with neighbors, each a small circle of tiny distant figures. Between the circles run strings of festival lights like the yarn on his old corkboard, visually joining circle to circle. First stars. The city reads as a community of communities, catching everyone. Lower-right: deep calm dusk sky. DAVID'S PROFILE IS TRUE TO HIS REFERENCES: a comparatively FLAT, even facial profile, straight moderate nose, firm chin that does not jut forward.
spreads._caption: What works in a room works in the world. A society is a community of communities, and it has edges too, crowded with people slipping through cracks. Hyperagents can build the systems that notice them, welcome them in, and waste nobody. That is the world worth building toward.
spreads.anonymous: Distant tiny neighborhood figures in the light circles, too small for faces; none distinct, none resembling David.
negatives: a second man resembling David near the camera
cold blue cityscape: every light is warm

spreads.scene: A warm evening block party fills the frame with ORDINARY PEOPLE AND THEIR SMALL HELPERS: at LEFT a silver-haired teacher sits on a folding chair reading to children while TWO CORAL HOLOGRAPHIC SUB-AGENTS in white sailor caps hold her picture books in a patient stack; at CENTER a doctor in scrubs laughs with a neighbor while a sub-agent at her elbow holds up a small stack of paper for her morning; at RIGHT neighbors string festival lights between porches while a sub-agent steadies the ladder and another carries the bulb bucket. Long tables, casseroles, kids chalking the pavement. Every agent is helping hands, never the hero. Dusk gold. Lower-right: chalk drawings on pavement, calm, no figures.
spreads._caption: The coming years belong to people like this. Teachers with a thousand patient helpers. Doctors whose agents read every new paper overnight. Neighbors who can organize a block as easily as a group chat. People who choose their evolution on purpose, and choose it for the rest of us too.
spreads.anonymous: The whole block: teacher, doctor, neighbors, children, all visibly distinct from one another; nobody resembles David and nobody wears a sky-blue button-down.

spreads.scene: A QUIET PROPHECY OF A PICTURE. In a wide, calm dusk landscape, THE PLAIN DOOR stands alone and slightly AJAR in the middle distance, warm light spilling through the gap, exactly as its reference plates hold it: plain honey-brown wood, four recessed panels, round brass knob, no lettering of any kind. DAVID KOBROSKY walks toward it along a gentle path, seen in three-quarter view from behind-left so his warm profile stays visible, unhurried, hands easy, HIS EYES ON THE DOOR and the light in the gap. The evening around him is soft rolling meadow and first stars; the light through the door is the warmest thing in the frame. Nothing shows what is behind the door. Lower-right: dusk grass, calm.
spreads._caption: And one more thing, spoken here as prophecy. Someday, when his amazing tour at Anthropic is complete, David will go and build one of the greatest consumer intelligence platforms of all time, a place where companies finally know the people they serve. But that is a story for another day.
negatives: any lettering, sign, or plaque on or near the door

spreads.scene: DAVID KOBROSKY alone, waist-up, warm and large just left of center, facing the VIEWER directly: the reader is the person he is meeting. His open hand reaches toward the camera in his signature welcome, close enough that the hand is gently soft-focus, his grinning face the sharp subject. Behind him, out of focus, the warm suggestion of the whole book: string lights, a corkboard of yarn, a faint coral glow at the edge. His expression is the one he saves for the person standing alone by the snack table: you, specifically, were exactly who this room was waiting for. Lower-right: soft warm bokeh, calm.
spreads._caption: So this book is an introduction too, the kind David never thinks to make for himself. Reader, here is a man who spends his days connecting people to people, founders to the future, and humanity to its own next chapter. David, meet everyone. Everyone, meet David. Let me introduce you.
negatives: salesman slickness: the warmth is personal, not performed
